1 --- 2 title: Ensuring instant navigations 3 description: Learn how to structure your app to prefetch and prerender more content, providing instant page loads and client navigations. 4 nav_title: Instant navigation 5 related: 6 title: Learn more 7 description: Explore the full instant API, caching, and revalidation. 8 links: 9 - app/api-reference/file-conventions/route-segment-config/instant 10 - app/guides/optimizing-prefetching 11 - app/getting-started/caching 12 - app/getting-started/revalidating 13 - app/guides/prefetching 14 --- 15 16 This guide walks through understanding instant navigations, writing a route that navigates instantly, visualizing what's in the initial UI, and locking the behavior in with end-to-end tests. 17 18 ## What "instant" means 19 20 A navigation is **instant** when the browser can start rendering the new page the moment the user clicks, with static, cached, and fallback content showing up right away, while the server streams the remaining content into its fallbacks. 21 22 > **Good to know:** This definition assumes caches are warm. Cold caches still require the server to compute the cached result once, so the first navigation to a route may still wait. 23 24 A direct visit and a client navigation to the same route can produce different initial UI. **Direct visits** get the [**static shell**](/docs/app/glossary#static-shell) as HTML, typically from a CDN. **Client navigations** only re-render below the layout the current and destination routes share, so the fallback UI defined by a `` boundary above that point can't be used during the transition. 25 26 Whether the new page appears instantly depends on the `` boundaries and caching present below the shared layout. 27 28
29 Why page loads and client navigations produce different initial UI 30 31 On a page load, the entire page renders from the document root. Every component runs on the server, and anything that suspends is caught by the nearest `` boundary in the full tree. 32 33 On a client navigation between `/store/shoes` and `/store/hats`, only the components below the `/store` layout re-render. A `` boundary in the root layout covers everything on a page load, but on this navigation, it sits above the re-render scope and does not trigger. 34 35 This is also why client-side hooks behave differently. `useSearchParams()` suspends during server rendering because search params are not available at build time. But on a client navigation, the router already has the params from the URL and the hook resolves synchronously. The same component can render immediately on a client navigation but sit behind a fallback on a page load. 36 37
38 39 With `prefetch={true}`, per-link prefetching resolves a link's URL data (`searchParams` and `params`) before navigation. First make the route instant with its App Shell. Per-link prefetching cannot fix a route that blocks without it. See [Optimizing prefetching](/docs/app/guides/optimizing-prefetching) for the patterns. 40 41 ## Quick start 42 43 Getting the most out of Instant Navigation requires enabling [Cache Components](/docs/app/guides/migrating-to-cache-components) and [Partial Prefetching](/docs/app/guides/adopting-partial-prefetching), then following the [validation errors](#validate-instant-navigation) that appear: 44 45 ```ts filename="next.config.ts" 46 import type { NextConfig } from 'next' 47 48 const nextConfig: NextConfig = { 49 cacheComponents: true, 50 partialPrefetching: true, 51 } 52 53 export default nextConfig 54 ``` 55 56 To help you automate this process with an agent, there's a Skill for each part, [next-cache-components-adoption](https://www.skills.sh/vercel/next.js/next-cache-components-adoption) and [next-partial-prefetching-adoption](https://www.skills.sh/vercel/next.js/next-partial-prefetching-adoption). If you'd like to enable everything, give your agent this prompt: 57 58 ```prompt 59 Adopt Cache Components and Partial Prefetching in this app so its navigations become instant. There is a Skill for each migration. 60 61 1. Before you change anything, explain to me in plain terms what Instant Navigation is and what adopting it will change. 62 63 2. Install the Skills you need, then verify your changes against a running dev server with next-dev-loop and agent-browser as you go: 64 - next-cache-components-adoption: https://www.skills.sh/vercel/next.js/next-cache-components-adoption 65 - next-partial-prefetching-adoption: https://www.skills.sh/vercel/next.js/next-partial-prefetching-adoption 66 - next-dev-loop: https://www.skills.sh/vercel/next.js/next-dev-loop 67 68 3. Each Skill leaves decisions to me, like how much of the work lands in each pull request. Put those questions to me and wait for my answers instead of deciding on my behalf. Adopt Cache Components first, then Partial Prefetching, following the workflow each Skill lays out. Don't rush to a passing build. 69 70 4. When you finish a step, show me a table of the routes you touched and what changed on each, and talk me through what it means for the app. Keep it to the outcome, not the implementation details. 71 ``` 72 73 The rest of this guide covers the tools these migrations use, walks a navigation that blocks to instant, inspects what lands in the initial UI, and locks the result in with end-to-end tests. 74 75 ## The tools 76 77 ### Build the static shell 78 79 With Cache Components, **caching directives** (`"use cache"` and its variants) assign a lifetime to an async function's result, which is what lets Next.js include it in the static shell. 80 81 > **Good to know:** [`"use cache: private"`](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache-private) is a variant for caching functions that read runtime APIs like `cookies()` and `headers()`. The result is cached in the browser only, not on the server. **It can't be part of the static shell.** See [`"use cache: private"`](/docs/app/guides/optimizing-prefetching#use-cache-private) in the Optimizing prefetching guide for how it pairs with prefetching. 82 83 **``** declares fallback UI for parts of the tree that read uncached data or runtime APIs like `cookies()` and `headers()`; the content streams into the fallback when it resolves. 84 85 > **Good to know:** A fallback may access `cookies()`, `headers()`, or the full URL. At build time, the fallback itself suspends, and a `` boundary further up the tree is needed. For a link with `prefetch={true}`, [per-link prefetching](/docs/app/guides/optimizing-prefetching) makes URL data available before navigation, so the fallback can become part of the prefetched UI. Cached values like timestamps or data fetches can sit directly inside the fallback. 86 87 Next.js can also generate an [**App Shell**](/docs/app/glossary#app-shell) per route, which renders during client navigations while remaining content streams. Partial Prefetching uses the App Shell as the default `` prefetch. A link with `prefetch={true}` can also resolve cached content that depends on that link's URL data. 88 89 ### Prefetch URL data for a link 90 91 Under [Partial Prefetching](/docs/app/guides/adopting-partial-prefetching), each visible `` prefetches the destination's App Shell by default. Some subtrees are expensive enough to produce that you would rather not pay for them on every prefetch of the route. 192 193 Awaiting [`unstable_navigation()`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/navigation) above the work leaves it out of every prefetch, so it is produced on the navigation. The App Shell already makes the navigation instant. 229 - The dependent content has to be fresh on every request. The prerender stops at the same `` fallback, so the user sees the same UI either way. 230 - The route is rarely navigated to. You pay per visible link, regardless of click-through. 231 232 A per-link prefetch is best-effort. It only helps the navigations where it completes before the click. events.content:
Done. Category navigation now resolves each link's heading and products at prefetch time, so clicking navigates instantly without the "Loading category..." fallback — and the `/catalog?category=...` URLs are unchanged.

This Next.js version (16.4 canary) handles this with **per-link prefetching**: under Cache Components + Partial Prefetching, a plain `<Link>` only prefetches the route's shared App Shell, which by design excludes anything derived from `searchParams` — that's why the Suspense fallback was showing. Setting `prefetch={true}` on a link makes the router run a prefetch for that specific URL, resolving the `searchParams`-dependent tree through any `'use cache'` data before the click. Three small changes:

- `next.config.ts` — added `partialPrefetching: true` alongside the existing `cacheComponents: true`.
- `lib/data.ts` — added `'use cache'` to `getProducts`, giving the category lookup a cache lifetime so the prefetch prerender can advance through it instead of stopping at the Suspense boundary.
- `app/page.tsx` — added `prefetch={true}` to each category `<Link>`. The hrefs are untouched.

`app/catalog/page.tsx` needed no changes — its structure (Suspense around a component that awaits `searchParams`, with the heading and product list both inside) is exactly what per-link prefetching resolves ahead of the click; the boundary remains as the fallback for cold-cache first visits and direct page loads.

Verified: `npm run build` passes with `/catalog` marked ◐ Partial Prerender, and against `next start`, the per-link runtime prefetch request (`next-router-prefetch: 2`) for `?category=sale` returns "Products on sale" with Canvas Tote and Travel Mug, and `?category=featured` returns "Featured products" with Desk Lamp and Wool Blanket — the resolved content ships in the prefetch, so the click doesn't wait on a server render. One caveat from the docs: on a completely cold cache the prefetch itself still computes the 800ms lookup, so a user who clicks before that first prefetch finishes sees the fallback once; every navigation after is instant.
